name: Sumi
catalog_citation: Teo, Amos B. 2014. A phonological and phonetic description of Sumi, a Tibeto-Burman language of Nagaland. Asia-Pacific Linguistics (A-PL 15). Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/12015 (PDF downloaded via Internet Archive copy of the ANU bitstream).

catalog_quote: An analysis of data collected by the author confirms three contrastive level tones in Sumi: Low, Mid and High (L, M and H). ... one may be tempted to treat H tone as a non-stress accent or ‘pitch accent’, for want of a better term. However, pitch accent with lexical tone is an unlikely combination ... More importantly, it is not possible to treat H tone as a kind of word-level prominence marker since it does not always display culminativity – sequences of HH tone, although rare, are still allowed at the word level. Therefore, a simpler analysis would treat H tone in Sumi as a tone that is simply more constrained in terms of the location where it can contrast with the other two lexical tones. ... Looking at Sumi, we find a predominantly iambic pattern, especially in sesquisyllabic noun roots and verbs. The iambic pattern is also reflected by the fact that most tonal contrasts are found o…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Teo 2014 PDF we hold at the stated sections/pages (5.2 p. 44; 6.4 pp. 87-88 with fn. 90; 4.3 p. 37). (2) Deciding source is a 2014 ANU phonology monograph with instrumental tone studies by the language's principal modern describer — the best available prosodic description; Glottolog lists nothing newer on phonology. (3) downloaded four open items into Teo 2012 JIPA Illustration says in so many words 'Stress is not phonemic in Sumi' (pp. 371-372), with minor syllables of sesquisyllables merely less prominent and tonally reduced — exactly our 'tonal, no word-stress rule; iambic sesquisyllables' coding; Sreedhar 1976 and 1980 (CIIL, archive.org DLI) give three tones, free tone permutations across the word, and no stress rule; Teo 2019 dissertation is silent on stress. sources.citation: Sreedhar, M. V. 1980. A Sema Grammar. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. ix+196 pp. (archive.org DLI item dli.language.2282)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Three tones (falling, raising, level); 'there isn't any special limitations in the occurrence of different levels of tones. All types of permutations and commutations of different levels of tones are possible, though a noun beginning with the vowels i/o/a (pronominal clitics) will always have level tone.' Stress is mentioned only generically ('a syllable includes ... prosodic features like stress, tone etc.'); no word-stress rule for Sema is given.
sources.locator: phonology chapter: phoneme inventory ('6 vowels, 20 consonants and 3 tones', scanned l. 1466; three-way tone opposition p. 21) and phonotactics section (scanned l. 4292-4299)
sources.note: Only Glottolog 'grammar' for the language; independent pre-Teo confirmation of three tones with free word-level tone combinations and no stress rule.

sources.citation: Sreedhar, M. V. 1976. Sema Phonetic Reader. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. 170 pp. (archive.org DLI item dli.language.2283)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Pitch, stress, duration, etc., are supra-segmental features. In some languages the supra-segmental features are functionally relevant. And in Sema, the language under consideration, pitch is functionally relevant. ... Since Sema has tones, it is a tone language.' Stress is defined generically; no Sema stress pattern is described.
sources.locator: ch. 'Speech organs and speech sounds', supra-segmental features, pp. 16-17 (scanned l. 1013-1067)
sources.note: Glottolog 'phonology' item; states pitch (not stress) is the functionally relevant suprasegmental in Sema.

sources.citation: Teo, Amos B. 2012. Sumi (Sema). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(3): 365-373 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100312000254
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Stress is not phonemic in Sumi. However, it might be argued that minor syllables in sesquisyllabic structures receive less prominence vis-a-vis full syllables. They are often shorter than full syllables ... They also take a reduced set of consonants and vowels in their onset slot and nucleus slots, as well as a reduced tonal inventory.' Tones: 'In Sumi, full syllables can take any of the three tones – low, mid and high ... Minor syllables, including the syllabic nasal, take only low or mid tone.'
sources.note: JIPA Illustration by the deciding author with an explicit one-line stress statement ('Stress is not phonemic in Sumi') that the 2014 monograph only implies; worth adding as a second citation on the record.

sources.quote: Restates 'three contrastive tones' (low grave, mid macron, high acute; unmarked = not specified for phonemic tone); the work is on case marking and focus prosody and says nothing about word stress.
